submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on words that open an explanatory or relational frame for what follows: abstract relational head nouns after 'the' (reasons/reason, implications, way, role, impact, importance, effects, causes, meaning; about 1.6-3.7), clause-introducing wh/relative words (how, where, why, what, which, relative 'that'; 1.4-2.8, highest after 'that is/that's'), sentence-initial Here/There/Where/Then after a previous sentence (1.5-3.8), passive-agent 'by' and cross-reference 'see' (about 2-3.4). It is a graded dial, so weaker activity at or just above the 0.25 x max line also occurs on 'on/of/at the' in descriptive phrases (1.0-1.8), some transitive verbs (discussed, studied, fixed, painted; 1.2-1.4), colour adjectives (about 1-1.8) and a sentence-final period (0.95-1.1, right at the line); predicted inactive (peak <= 0.50 on 24 measured examples) are short everyday yes/no questions ending in '?' that use possessives (your/my) instead of 'the' and contain none of these words, e.g. 'Did you lock your front door last night?'.

Everything You Need to Know About How Industrial Ball Valves Operate
A high-quality valve is essential whether you’re transporting liquids, solids, or gases. It regulates flow and provides a range of other functions. There are several types, each suited to different kinds of projects. The market for ball valves is growing rapidly. At a compound annual growth rate or CAGR of 3.75%, they’re expected to become a $15.2 billion industry by 2024.
What makes these particular types of valves so popular? Why do professionals choose them when there are so many other options on the market? How do they operate?
Read our guide to ball valves for the answers to these questions and more.
What Is a Ball Valve?
Before knowing how to use ball valves and why you should consider installing them, it’s important to understand exactly what they are.
An industrial valve is part of a machine used to control the flow of liquids, solids, and/or gases. Ball valves are a common type.
A ball valve is similar to a plug valve but distinguishable by the ball-shaped seating element it’s named after.
Ball valves are known as quarter-turn valves because they only require a 25-degree turn to switch from on to off and back again. This makes them much easier to operate than other types of valves.
Check out a ball valve diagram online for more information on the parts that make them up.
Ball Valve Types
There are several types of valves used in industrial and home settings. Understanding the differences between them all helps you choose the best one for your project.
Top-entry ball valves allow for easy repair and maintenance by removing the bonnet-cover. An end-entry valve has a single-piece body, making it harder to repair.
Ball valves can be lubricated with a similar lubricant-seal system to those found in plug valves. They can also be non-lubricated.
Ball valves can also be classified as floating-ball, trunion-mounted, welded body or orbit ball.
The floating-ball setup leaves the ball free to move as a result of fluid pressure. They create a tight seal but aren’t best for high-pressure situations or large pipes. This is due to potentially damaging high force and difficulty of operation.
Trunion-mounted ball valves let their balls rotate in a fixed position. A shaft at the top and bottom keeps the ball in place, allowing these valves to be used at higher pressures and in larger sizes. They also require less force to operate.
Orbit ball valves rotate to create a seal. They require more turns to move but are easier to operate and cheaper at larger sizes or in high-powered setups.
Ball valves can be classified by the type of bore they have. Free-flow is an expensive option used when free-flowing liquids are required. Reduced-bore occurs when the port in the ball is smaller, reducing flow.

Micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) are systems which are developed using thin film technology and which include both electrical and micro mechanical components. MEMS devices are used in a variety of applications such as optical display systems, pressure sensors, flow sensors, and charge control actuators. MEMS devices use electrostatic force or energy to move or monitor the movement of micro-mechanical components. In one type of MEMS device, to achieve a desired result, a gap distance between electrodes is controlled by balancing an electrostatic force and a mechanical restoring force. Typically, digital MEMS devices use two discrete gap distances while analog MEMS devices use variable gap distances.
Such MEMS devices have been developed using a variety of approaches. In one approach, a deformable deflective membrane is positioned over an electrode and is electrostatically attracted to the electrode. Other approaches use flaps or beams of silicon or aluminum, which form a top conducting layer. With optical applications, the conducting layer is reflective while the deflective membrane is deformed using electrostatic force to direct light, which is incident upon the conducting layer.
One approach for controlling the gap distance between electrodes is to apply a continuous control voltage to the electrodes, wherein the control voltage is increased to decrease the gap distance, and vice-versa. However, this approach suffers from electrostatic instability that greatly reduces a useable operating range over which the gap distance can be effectively controlled. In addition, the speed with which the gap distance may be changed depends primarily on the physical characteristics of the MEMS device. When the voltage is changed, the gap distance between the electrodes lags the change of voltage as the MEMS device settles to its final position.
